idiom_name: kotlin.Result with map/fold; flatMap via fold or an extension
implementation_notes: Kotlin's stdlib Result<T> is a value class carrying either a value or a Throwable: runCatching turns a throwing expression into a Result (unit), map transforms the success side, and fold collapses both sides - but stdlib defines no flatMap, so bind is written with fold or a small extension (fun <T, R> Result<T>.flatMap(f: (T) -> Result<R>): Result<R>). Nullable types with ?. and the elvis operator cover the Maybe instance, and Arrow's Either is the library route when a typed error channel and real monad instances are required.
pitfalls: kotlin.Result is deliberately constrained (it cannot wrap another Result and is designed for return values), so it is not a general-purpose monad container.
runCatching catches Throwable, including CancellationException, which breaks coroutine cancellation if used around suspending calls.
Because stdlib lacks flatMap, every module tends to grow its own variant of the extension; centralise one implementation.

variants.name: Suspend functions + await (IO as coroutines)
variants.implementation_notes: The IO instance in Kotlin is the coroutine: a suspend function yields the eventual value and awaiting it suspends until the previous step completes, so dependent I/O reads as straight-line code without a monad type. Structured concurrency (coroutineScope, async) controls the concurrency, and cancellation is a first-class failure mode; combine it with Result only at API boundaries where errors must be values.
pitfalls: Suspend functions need a coroutine scope; GlobalScope bypasses structured concurrency and leaks work.
Blocking calls (JDBC, Thread.sleep) inside a coroutine block the dispatcher thread; move them to withContext(Dispatchers.IO).
Cancellation is cooperative: loops and blocking sections must check for cancellation or they ignore it.
